conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time for this today. I’m <med>Dr. Maya Rivera</med>, a perinatal-mental-health clinician who works with new mothers. To keep things simple, you can call me Maya.  

The short questionnaire we’re about to do is called the <sym>Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale</sym>—usually shortened to the <sym>EPDS</sym>. It’s a 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past seven days of new motherhood. It also checks whether you’re having any thoughts that might be hard to talk about, so we can be sure you have the right support.  

Everything you share stays confidential within the clinical team unless you tell us you’re in immediate danger; then our goal is safety and we’d talk together about next steps. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. Each question can be answered in a few words, and we’ll move through all ten in just a couple of minutes.  

When you’re ready, we’ll begin.  

1. Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things the way you usually do, or has that felt difficult?
No, not really… I mean, I’ll smile if someone makes a joke, but I don’t feel that real laugh inside. Things that used to crack me up just feel flat lately.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I wish I could say that. Most of the time, even when my partner tries to be funny, I just give a little smile—it's like the joy part is missing.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Not really… I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even a favorite show—but this week it’s mostly “why bother.” I still do them, yet the spark isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong or I’m not a good enough mom. I’ll replay everything in my head and find some way it must be my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing, imagining she’s too quiet or too warm, or that I’ll drop her. Nothing’s actually wrong, but I can’t shake the “what-ifs” until I check her breathing three or four times.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, it hits out of nowhere—like a tight band around my chest when I’m just folding laundry. My mind jumps to her choking or something happening while I’m in the bathroom, and I feel shaky until I peek into the crib again.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah... most days it feels like I'm drowning in small stuff. The dishes pile up, she won't nap unless I'm holding her, and I keep thinking, "How does everyone else manage?" I get through it, but it feels like I'm barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I’ve been lying there after her 2 a.m. feed, mind racing—worrying I’m doing everything wrong, replaying every little fuss—so even when she’s asleep I can’t drift off. Takes me at least an hour, sometimes two, and then I start listening for her again.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah… sad is kind of my normal this week. I tear up over tiny things—like running out of diapers or seeing a cute onesie—and the low mood just sits there even when I try to distract myself.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Uh-huh, I’ve cried three times since last weekend—once when she wouldn’t latch, once when my mom left after visiting, and once while I was just staring at the wall feeling useless. It’s not all-day sobbing, but the tears come pretty easily.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I feel low, but I’d never want to leave her or hurt myself.

You've shared that the joy you once felt has slipped away-laughter feels flat, excitement is replaced by <sym>apathy</sym>, and most days you're weighed down by a persistent <sym>low mood</sym> and daily tears. You describe frequent <sym>anxiety</sym> and sudden <sym>panic</sym> even when your baby is safe, and nights are long because worries race through your mind. Despite this, you clearly care deeply for your little one, and you've firmly rejected any self-harm thoughts.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only a faint smile and a loss of joy, indicating a clear but not total inability to laugh</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-complete loss of anticipatory joy, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame 'a lot' with repetitive, pervasive guilt about motherhood performance, aligning with 'most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, disproportionate worries about infant safety that compel repeated checking—clearly matching "very often".</sym>, <sym>Yes, quite a lot'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and difficulty coping, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling back to sleep for 1–2 hours due to racing worries, matching "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent sadness as her "normal" this week, frequent tearfulness, and inability to lift mood—clearly aligns with "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes tied to distressing events, indicating crying "quite often" but not "most of the time.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 24 (range 0-30) places you well above the 13+ cutoff that signals probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Within the past seven days you endorse core depressive symptoms-<sym>markedly reduced pleasure</sym>, <sym>daily sadness</sym>, <sym>frequent crying</sym>, <sym>guilt-ridden rumination</sym>-plus prominent <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>nocturnal insomnia</sym> linked to racing worries. These findings parallel <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for a major depressive episode, and the postpartum timing (< 4 weeks) supports the peripartum specifier. Although you denied self-harm (Q10 score 0), the combined emotional distress and functional impact (feeling you're "drowning" in routine tasks) warrant urgent evaluation and treatment planning. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>midwife</med>, or <med>primary care provider</med> within the next few days for full assessment and care planning
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med>, <med>CBT</med>, or <med>sertraline</med> which are compatible with breastfeeding if chosen
3. Share practical support needs-accept help with housework, meals, or night feeds so you can rest; aim for at least one 4-hour stretch of sleep in 24 h
4. Try brief calming strategies when panic surges: slow diaphragmatic breathing, 5-4-3-2-1 grounding, or a short paced walk with baby in carrier
5. Keep the baby-care routine simple: one outing or visitor per day, leave dishes for later, and celebrate small wins (shower, eaten meal)
6. Schedule a follow-up EPDS or PHQ-9 in one week to monitor progress after starting interventions
7. If distress escalates or you ever feel unsafe, go to the nearest emergency department or call your local mental-health crisis line
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Screening note – Postpartum visit  
Date: [today]

Patient-reported symptoms (last 7 days)

Affect/pleasure  
- Marked anhedonia: minimal laughter, loss of anticipatory enjoyment  
- Persistent low mood with daily tearfulness (3 discrete crying episodes)  

Cognition  
- Pervasive self-blame/guilt re parenting competence  
- Frequent rumination at night interfering with return to sleep (≥60–120 min delay after infant feeds)

Anxiety  
- Daily unprovoked worry (infant safety), episodic chest tightness/shakiness consistent with panic symptoms  
- Multiple reassurance behaviors (re-checks breathing, crib peeks)

Functional  
- Feels “drowning” in routine tasks; describes “barely treading water”

Safety  
- Denies any self-harm thoughts or intent

Pattern: symptoms present most of the day, nearly every day since last week; cause subjective distress and mild impairment in sleep, mood, and task management.  
Screening significance: meets threshold for probable postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety; no acute safety risk identified at this time.

Next step: recommend formal clinical interview (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS) and follow-up within 1 week for further evaluation and care planning.
